summary: The visible notes of the map swept into the island's own voice: 31 marker notes (record 35) that still carried the generator's stock wording (inns, lighthouses, pirates, circus, fair, springs, battlefields and the rest) rewritten from the annals of each place, keeping every dish, date, number and name they held; and the 13 regiments' and fleets' notes (record 14) as lines of the regimental roll (raised DE 21, station, strength in DE 27). Each note is set whole; the earlier edits of the same notes are set aside (skip), so a second run changes nothing.

map_edits.value: Warm springs below Muileann ruadh, whose water comes up out of the mountain at about a hundred and four degrees of the humans' scale. The sick have been bathed here since the Ancient Age for their ease and their healing, and the bath-house over the basins takes in the sick of every rite.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: A holy stream in the east. It is told that whoever drinks of it in the right quarter of the moon will have good fortune, and pilgrims of every rite have walked to it since the Holy Age. Its water is clear as glass and carries a sheen of many colours that glints even in the dimmest light, and it is said never to have failed.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: A stone bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg, rebuilt and widened more than once on the same piers. Queen Sìleas's name is cut on the downstream parapet.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: An old stone crossing of the river above Ros fhionn, first built by Ailean Clachair, whose hearth-sign is still sharp in the keystone. Few have used it since the trade of the district fell away.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: A great road-house of the old mining roads, and one of the best known. Its first keeper was Mòr nic Dhùghaill, a widow of Doire shean, and it still serves her jugged buffalo, with shiny water to drink. The War of the Roads was ended under its roof.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: A great road-house on the eastern road, where the carriers from Cnoc leathan meet the southern coast path. It faces south and is known for its warmth, for the songs of Fearchar Bàrd, and for pan-fried spinach with black wine, which it once set before the queen's progress.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: A great road-house on the northern road above Inis mhòr, raised by Catrìona Ghlic for the carriers of the Hall's baskets. It serves oatcakes fried in linseed oil, with the barley spirit the carriers call fire water.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: A great stone road-house on the bare moor of the northern road, built for carriers caught by the snow. Its fare is pickled spinach with fire milk; a party of reeves once lived on nothing else through a whole season snowed in.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: A great road-house on the eastern road north of Seann Dunn, the first to be raised by a ruler's order, by Mòrag nan Rathad. It is known for syrupped beef, served with hot juice.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The great road-house at the halfway stage of the central mining road, where the ox-teams of the mountain wait out the snow. The brothers Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn made their peace under its roof. It serves steamed carp with green brandy.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The far-off house on the eastern road near the silver country, so far from any town that carriers say one is never nearer to it than halfway. The road-peace was first kept here, and no feud may be followed under its roof. Its fare is dried deer with black water.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The sea-light on the north-western headland at Baile chrom, the last of the five towers to be built. A fire was kept on this headland in the Ancient Age to warn boats off the water where the Sea-Watcher was seen; the tower is a beacon for ships in the open sea.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The sea-light on the eastern cape at Baile ìseal, the second of the five towers. The households of the coast kept a fire here in the Ancient Age to bring the boats home in a storm, and the tower is a beacon for ships in the open sea.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The sea-light on the northern point at Muileann bheag, the fourth of the five towers and the first to burn ore. The ash of the old shore-fire lies three yards deep beneath it. It is a beacon for ships in the open sea.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The sea-light on the north-eastern cape at Àth dhearg, the third of the five towers, marking the passage in toward Seann Tarr. Its keeper Tormod mac Pheadair kept a daybook of every ship he saw. It is a beacon for ships in the open sea.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The sea-light on the southern cape at Tobar dhearg, the first of the five towers. Here the island's first sea-light was raised above the ground, a stone tower with the fire on its top, and it is a beacon for ships in the open sea.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The field of the last great battle of An Cogadh Fada, the Long War, fought on 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22. The first and third regiments stood here, and the holdouts were broken.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The field of the first great battle of An Cogadh Fada, the Long War, fought on 11 an Giblean, DE 21. It has been left unploughed, and the Tuathaich have raised a cairn on it.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: Uilebheist na Mara, the Sea-Watcher. Sailors have told of a great beast in these dangerous waters since the Ancient Age, and boats of Baile chrom have been lost here in a calm sea. Some say it is thirty feet long.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: Marbh-bheò, the Hollow Man of the Doire uaine hills. Old inscriptions there tell of a thing that walks without breath and falls on any who dare come near its lair or light a fire in its sight. No fire is lit where these hills can see it.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The raiders' water off the north-west coast. Outlaws put off in boats here in the Holy Age and lived by plundering the fishing strands, and raiders' ships have been seen in these waters in every age since.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The raiders' water off the east coast. Outlaws have raided the eastern strands from the islets offshore since the Holy Age. In the Age of Strangers they burned a Company ore ship here and ran rifles for the silver guild, and their low black boats are still seen.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The raiders' bays off Cathair gheal on the north-west coast. Raiders have taken the dried fish from these strands since the Holy Age. The fourth fleet found the bays empty after the Long War, but the fishermen say the raiders will be back.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: Ruins of a walled outpost of the Old Ones on a spur above Cathair mhòr. Its stones are dressed on the outer face only, and its single gate faces inland and was blocked with rubble from the inside. Who built it is not known.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The great library of Muileann chaol, founded in the Age of the Kingdom, with Ailean Leabhar for its first keeper. It holds the fullest record of the island's history that has come down, and many rare and ancient books. 'A chur san Leabharlann', to put it in the Library, is said of anything settled beyond dispute.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn, the travelling circus that no one understands, pitched on the common near Inis àrsaidh. It stays only a little while and moves on. The magistrate who licensed it entered its acts as 'various'.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn, the travelling circus that no one understands, where it was first seen, on the southern coast near Seann Chwen. It never stays long, and no one has yet said what its acts are meant to show.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The field of the Còmhrag at Ceann leathan. Fighters come from all over the island to its yearly melee, and men have died in it. The winner takes fame and fortune, and the crowd's favour.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: The fair of Muileann òg, held at the ford where the Stone King Raghnall Ceannfhionn and the holder of the Red Hill agreed salt for wool, the oldest meeting-place on the island. Goods of Rodos and of lands over the sea change hands here, and every craft and service is to be had.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: Cidhe Beag, the little quay: an old landing on the Abhainn uaine, where boats have been put into the river since the Ancient Age. A ferryman keeps it, a weary-looking man, and he will sell passage along the river.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, the old burial ground on the hill, whose oldest graves are older than any name that can be read. The thorn grows back over the stones faster than the keepers can clear it, the flowers fade among them, and it is said that the dead walk there and mourn.
map_edits.why: the note in the voice of the island's place-lore, drawn from the annals of the place

map_edits.value: Raised in DE 21, the first year of An Cogadh Fada, the Long War, and stationed at Inis mhòr. In DE 27 it musters 826 foot, 581 horse, 398 riflemen and 13 guns.
map_edits.why: the regiment's note as a line of the regimental roll, same year, station and strength
